Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Models

Source: vignettes/spatial-temporal.Rmd
spatial-temporal.Rmd

Overview

When small areas are geographic units (such as counties, regencies, or districts), spatial correlation frequently occurs: neighboring areas tend to have more similar outcomes than distant ones. Furthermore, when surveys are repeated over multiple years, temporal correlation between time periods is also present.

fastsae provides specialized, high-performance implementations for both: 1. Spatial Fay-Herriot (eblup_sfh): Simultaneous Autoregressive SAR(1) random effects. 2. Spatio-Temporal Fay-Herriot (eblup_stfh): Combined spatial SAR(1) and temporal AR(1) random effects.

1. Spatial Fay-Herriot Model (eblup_sfh)

Model Formulation

The Spatial Fay-Herriot model (Pratesi & Salvati, 2008) models area random effects using a Simultaneous Autoregressive (SAR(1)) process:

y=Xβ+u+ey = X\beta + u + e

u=ρ1Wu+ϵ1⟹u=(I−ρ1W)−1ϵ1u = \rho_1 W u + \epsilon_1 \implies u = (I - \rho_1 W)^{-1} \epsilon_1

where: - WW is a known row-standardized spatial proximity matrix (D×DD \times D). - ρ1∈(−1,1)\rho_1 \in (-1, 1) is the spatial autoregressive parameter. - ϵ1∼N(0,σu12ID)\epsilon_1 \sim N(0, \sigma_{u1}^2 I_D) is independent innovation noise. - e∼N(0,Ve)e \sim N(0, V_e) is sampling error with diagonal matrix Ve=diag(D1,…,DD)V_e = \text{diag}(D_1, \dots, D_D).

Fitting the Model 

library(fastsae)
data("mys")
data("mys_proxmat")

# Fit Spatial Fay-Herriot model with REML
fit_sfh <- eblup_sfh(
  formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  vardir = ~vardir,
  data = mys,
  W = mys_proxmat,
  method = "REML",
  print_result = FALSE
)

summary(fit_sfh)
#> 
#> ── Summary of fastsae Fit ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Call :
#> eblup_sfh(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = ~vardir, data = mys, method =
#> "REML", W = mys_proxmat, print_result = FALSE)

#> x2           0.0568516  0.0525488  1.0818827 0.2793

Unsampled Domains and Spatial Kriging

A major advantage of eblup_sfh in fastsae is its automatic handling of unsampled domains (domains with y = NA). Instead of throwing an error or requiring manual subsetting, eblup_sfh automatically performs full-spatial kriging:

# Count sampled vs unsampled domains
table(is.na(mys$y))
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>    32    10

# Inspect estimates for unsampled domains
head(fit_sfh$df_eblup[is.na(mys$y), ])
#>    domain  y vardir    eblup random_effect      mse      rse
#> 21     21 NA      0 4.136624    0.33273263 1.773635 32.19482
#> 25     25 NA      0 3.666578   -0.63352730 1.606281 34.56606
#> 26     26 NA      0 6.293404    0.82251711 1.962186 22.25792
#> 27     27 NA      0 5.185438    0.66260236 1.879788 26.44046
#> 28     28 NA      0 5.159499   -0.02771458 1.448608 23.32748
#> 34     34 NA      0 3.834916    0.17166576 1.587847 32.85856

For unsampled areas, prediction borrows strength from both the regression synthetic component xd⊤β̂x_d^\top \hat{\beta} and spatial proximity to neighboring sampled areas through (I−ρ̂1W)−1(I - \hat{\rho}_1 W)^{-1}.

Multi-Threaded Bootstrap MSE

In addition to analytical Prasad-Rao style MSE, eblup_sfh supports multi-threaded OpenMP bootstrap MSE estimation:

  • Parametric Bootstrap (mse_type = "pbmse")
  • Non-Parametric Bootstrap (mse_type = "npbmse")
fit_sfh_pb <- eblup_sfh(
  formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  vardir = ~vardir,
  data = mys,
  W = mys_proxmat,
  mse_type = "pbmse",
  B = 50,
  n_threads = 2,
  seed = 123,
  print_result = FALSE
)
#> ℹ 10 unsampled domain(s) detected. Bootstrap MSE (pbmse) is computed for the 32 sampled domain(s); unsampled domain(s) get a full-spatial synthetic (kriging) prediction and analytical MSE instead.

head(fit_sfh_pb$df_eblup[, c("domain", "y", "eblup", "mse", "mse_pb", "mse_pbbc")])
#>   domain        y    eblup       mse    mse_pb  mse_pbbc
#> 1      1 8.359527 7.535193 0.4999462 0.5838185 0.5822064
#> 2      2 7.599650 6.564385 0.5831410 0.7059036 0.6571795
#> 3      3 5.514137 5.109460 0.6095214 0.7555265 0.6814817
#> 4      4 3.869326 4.273391 0.5018535 0.5742035 0.5552008
#> 5      5 6.305063 6.791422 0.7644430 0.7705470 0.8859110
#> 6      6 3.926807 4.016701 0.3398919 0.3798275 0.3712704

2. Spatio-Temporal Fay-Herriot Model (eblup_stfh)

Model Formulation

The Spatio-Temporal model (Marhuenda, Molina, & Morales, 2013) combines spatial correlation and temporal autoregression for DD areas over TT time periods. The panel does not need to be complete: cells without a direct estimate are predicted (see below).

ydt=xdt⊤β+u1d+u2dt+edty_{dt} = x_{dt}^\top \beta + u_{1d} + u_{2dt} + e_{dt}

where: - u1=(u11,…,u1D)⊤u_1 = (u_{11}, \dots, u_{1D})^\top captures static spatial effects: u1=ρ1Wu1+ϵ1u_1 = \rho_1 W u_1 + \epsilon_1. - u2d=(u2d1,…,u2dT)⊤u_{2d} = (u_{2d1}, \dots, u_{2dT})^\top captures dynamic temporal effects for area dd: u2dt=ρ2u2d,t−1+ϵ2dtu_{2dt} = \rho_2 u_{2d,t-1} + \epsilon_{2dt}. - edt∼ind. N(0,Ddt)e_{dt} \sim \text{ind. } N(0, D_{dt}) are sampling errors.

The model is defined on the full D×TD \times T grid: u1u_1 on all domains of WW, u2u_2 on all periods.

Fitting the Spatio-Temporal Model 

data("mys_panel")

# 42 domains x 11 years; y is NA for the two domains that are never sampled
table(sampled = !is.na(mys_panel$y))
#> sampled
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>    22   440

# Fit Spatio-Temporal model with the analytical MSE, on the full panel and full W
fit_stfh <- eblup_stfh(
  formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x3,
  data = mys_panel,
  vardir = ~vardir,
  domain = ~area,
  time = ~year,
  W = mys_proxmat,
  model = "ST",
  mse_type = "analytical",
  print_result = FALSE
)

summary(fit_stfh)
#> 
#> ── Summary of fastsae Fit ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Call :
#> eblup_stfh(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = ~vardir, data = mys_panel,
#> domain = ~area, time = ~year, W = mys_proxmat, model = "ST", mse_type =
#> "analytical", print_result = FALSE)
#> 
#> ✔ Convergence: Yes (in 11 iterations)
#> Model: Spatio-Temporal Fay-Herriot (SAR + AR(1) time effects)
#> Method: REML
#> Cells without a direct estimate: 22 of 462 (predicted from the model)
#> 
#> Variance & Correlation Components:
#>    estimate  std.error
#>   2.2066952 0.64896010
#>  -0.9011506 0.31237444
#>   0.0000000 0.02602554
#>   0.7526384         NA
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                   beta  std.error     zvalue pvalue
#> (Intercept)  4.4442780  0.4445132  9.9980779 0.0000
#> x1          -0.0008817  0.0060240 -0.1463646 0.8836
#> x2           0.0254871  0.0277726  0.9177081 0.3588
#> x3           0.0163716  0.0256365  0.6386035 0.5231
#> 
#> Goodness of Fit:
#> loglikelihood           AIC           BIC 
#>     -597.2647     1210.5294     1243.2236 
#> 
#> EBLUP Summary Statistics:
#>       mse               rse          
#>  Min.   :0.03199   Min.   :   2.997  
#>  1st Qu.:0.08171   1st Qu.:   5.256  
#>  Median :0.11107   Median :   6.117  
#>  Mean   :0.25728   Mean   :  29.722  
#>  3rd Qu.:0.16233   3rd Qu.:   9.613  
#>  Max.   :2.47830   Max.   :2521.153

The estimated variance and correlation components include: - sigma21: Spatial random effect variance (σu12\sigma_{u1}^2). - rho1: Spatial autocorrelation (ρ1\rho_1). - sigma22: Temporal random effect variance (σu22\sigma_{u2}^2). - rho2: Temporal AR(1) autoregression coefficient (ρ2\rho_2).

The analytical MSE is g1+g2+2g3−g4g_1 + g_2 + 2 g_3 - g_4 (Prasad-Rao type, with the exact derivative of the EBLUP in g3g_3 and the curvature term g4g_4 for the nonlinear ρ1\rho_1, ρ2\rho_2); the components are returned as fit_stfh$g1, …, fit_stfh$g4. A parametric bootstrap MSE is available with mse_type = "bootstrap" (and B, seed).

Unsampled Domains and Missing Periods

Rows whose response is NA are kept and predicted, as long as the auxiliary variables are known there. The variance components are estimated from the sampled cells only (the marginal likelihood with the missing cells integrated out), and each missing cell gets the best linear unbiased predictor given the sampled data (Saei & Chambers, 2005; Benedetti et al., 2024):

  • a missing period of a sampled domain borrows from the other periods of that domain (AR(1) correlation) and from the neighbouring domains (SAR);
  • a domain that is never sampled is predicted from its neighbours only (spatial kriging), so W must keep it.
est <- fit_stfh$df_eblup
# Cells predicted without a direct estimate
head(est[!est$sampled, c("domain", "time", "eblup", "mse", "rse")])
#>     domain time    eblup      mse      rse
#> 21      21 2016 6.356729 2.389320 24.31664
#> 25      25 2016 3.225462 2.405876 48.08889
#> 63      21 2017 6.367907 2.385248 24.25326
#> 67      25 2017 3.213502 2.416602 48.37534
#> 105     21 2018 6.361026 2.389905 24.30319
#> 109     25 2018 3.174470 2.438947 49.19602

# Their MSE is larger: no direct estimate, only borrowed strength
tapply(est$mse, ifelse(est$sampled, "sampled", "unsampled"), median)
#>   sampled unsampled 
#> 0.1084668 2.4016341

For these cells the analytical MSE is g1+g2+g3g_1 + g_2 + g_3 (g3g_3 from the exact derivative of the predictor in the variance components); the bootstrap generates the random effects on the full grid and covers every cell too.

3. Comparing Models with autoplot

You can directly compare EBLUP estimates and uncertainty across different models using autoplot():

# Compare Fay-Herriot vs Spatial Fay-Herriot
fit_fh <- eblup_fh(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = ~vardir, data = na.omit(mys), print_result = FALSE)
W_clean <- mys_proxmat[!is.na(mys$y), !is.na(mys$y)]
fit_sfh_clean <- eblup_sfh(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = ~vardir, data = na.omit(mys), W = W_clean, print_result = FALSE)
#> Warning: `W` is not row-standardised: some rows do not sum to 1.
#> ℹ The SAR model with rho in (-1, 1) assumes rows summing to 1; use `W /
#>   rowSums(W)` or `create_weights(style = "W")`.

autoplot(list("Standard FH" = fit_fh, "Spatial FH" = fit_sfh_clean), type = "comparison")

4. Bayesian Spatio-Temporal Modeling (hb_area)

In addition to frequentist C++ EBLUP implementations (eblup_sfh and eblup_stfh), fastsae provides hb_area() for Bayesian spatio-temporal modeling powered by INLA. This supports: - Bounded proportions via Beta regression (matching tipsae) - Discrete counts via Poisson and Negative Binomial regression - Binary aggregates via Binomial regression - Flexible space-time structures including domain-specific random walks, separable dynamic fields, and Knorr-Held Types I–IV.

For full details and a case study on Italian poverty data, see the vignette Bayesian Area-Level Small Area Estimation with INLA.

References

  • Benedetti, R., Piersimoni, F., Pratesi, M., Salvati, N., & Suesse, T. (2024). Handling out-of-sample areas to estimate the unemployment rate at local labour market areas in Italy. International Statistical Review. https://doi.org/10.1111/insr.12596
  • Marhuenda, Y., Molina, I., & Morales, D. (2013). Small area estimation with spatio-temporal Fay-Herriot models. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 58, 308–325.
  • Pratesi, M., & Salvati, N. (2008). Small area estimation: The EBLUP estimator based on spatially correlated random area effects. Statistical Methods & Applications, 17(1), 113–141.
  • Saei, A., & Chambers, R. (2005). Out of sample estimation for small areas using area level data. Southampton Statistical Sciences Research Institute, Methodology Working Paper M05/11.
